They are complementary black-box techniques, and in practice BVA is applied on top of the classes that EP defines.

- Equivalence partitioning (EP) divides the input domain into equivalence classes — groups of values the program should treat identically. study_guide:equivalence partitioning.raw:
## What Equivalence Partitioning Is

- Equivalence partitioning (EP) divides the input domain of a program into equivalence classes: groups of values the program is expected to treat identically [1].
- The core assumption is that testing one representative value from each class reveals the same faults as testing every member of that class, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases [1].
- EP is described as a way to shrink a test suite while still covering every behaviourally distinct category of input [1].

## Valid and Invalid Partitions

- Partitions are drawn from both valid and invalid inputs [1].
- A complete test set samples at least one value from each class, valid and invalid alike [1].

## Worked Example: An Age Field

- For an age field that accepts 0 to 120, the valid class is the range 0 to 120 [1].
- The same field has two invalid classes: negative values, and values above 120 [1].
- A complete test set for this field therefore samples at least one value from the valid class and at least one from each of the two invalid classes [1].

## Combining Several Inputs

- When a program takes several inputs, EP considers each input's classes independently and then combines representative values [1].
- The combination is usually done with an all-combinations or pairwise strategy [1].
- The resulting test suite is much smaller than exhaustive testing but still covers every behaviourally distinct category of input [1].

## Pairing EP with Boundary Value Analysis

- Boundary value analysis (BVA) is a black-box technique that designs test cases around the edges of the input domain, since programmers most often make mistakes at the boundaries of a range: the minimum, the maximum, and the values immediately inside and outside them [2].
- BVA pairs naturally with equivalence partitioning: EP first divides the input domain into classes of values that should behave the same, and then BVA picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors are most likely to hide [2].
- For a field accepting integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA suggests testing 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101 [2].
- The classic three-point rule tests the minimum, minimum minus one and minimum plus one, plus the maximum, maximum minus one and maximum plus one, which yields six test cases [2].
- Practical reading: use EP to choose which classes to cover, then use BVA to choose the specific values at the edges of those classes [1][2].

## Key Takeaways

- EP = split the input domain into classes of values expected to behave the same, then test one representative per class [1].
- Always include invalid classes, not just valid ones [1].
- With multiple inputs, partition each input separately, then combine representatives (all-combinations or pairwise) [1].
- EP reduces test count without losing behaviourally distinct coverage [1].
- EP and BVA are complementary: EP defines the classes, BVA probes their edges [2].

Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.

## Quantum Entanglement

This isn't covered in your course materials, so here's a general explanation:

- Quantum entanglement is a relationship between two or more particles whose quantum states cannot be described independently of one another, even when the particles are physically separated.
- Entangled particles are described by a single shared state, so a measurement made on one particle is correlated with the result of a measurement on its partner in a way that classical physics cannot account for.
- These correlations are stronger than any explanation based on pre-existing "hidden" properties shared by the particles, a result captured by Bell's theorem and confirmed by experiments.
- Entanglement does not allow faster-than-light communication: the individual measurement outcomes still look random, and the correlations only become visible when the two sets of results are compared through ordinary (slower-than-light) communication.
- Entanglement is a physical resource used in quantum computing, quantum cryptography (such as quantum key distribution), and quantum teleportation.
- Important caveat: the passages supplied for this study guide cover software testing topics (boundary value analysis, equivalence partitioning, statement and branch coverage), not physics, so review your actual course notes or textbook if this topic is examinable.

passages.heading: Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
passages.text:
Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

Branch coverage is often called decision coverage. It subsumes statement coverage:
reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.

## Revisit

Boundary Value Analysis. Students are still working through where the edges of an input domain actually sit, so it is worth re-walking the core idea next class: why faults cluster at the minimum, the maximum, and the values just inside and just outside a range [1]. Re-run the worked example of an integer field accepting 1 to 100, and be explicit about why 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101 are the chosen values and why the three-point rule produces six test cases [1]. It would also help to show, step by step, how equivalence partitioning divides the domain first and how BVA then picks values at the edges of each class, and to make clear that these two techniques are meant to be used together rather than as alternatives [1].

Nothing. All of the topics raised map onto the existing material on Boundary Value Analysis [1], so no new material needs to be written before the next class.
